name: Social media dysmorphia (filter dysmorphia / Snapchat dysmorphia)

lead: Social media dysmorphia, also called filter or Snapchat dysmorphia, describes people who want to look like their filtered selfies. It drives interest in cosmetic procedures and in how photos are framed and edited. The term was coined by British surgeon Tijion Esho, who saw patients shift from bringing celebrity photos to edited images of themselves.

The chain: edit or filter selfies, wish to match the edited look, then seek procedures or change presentation. Filters smooth skin and reshape features in real time. Observational studies link photo editing and image-focused platform use to body dissatisfaction and willingness to consider surgery, though much of the evidence is correlational.

paras: People bring edited selfies to consultations, try filters before choosing procedures, or adjust lighting, angles and framing to get closer to the edited look. Clinicians discuss it alongside body dysmorphic disorder.

It is an informal term, not a diagnosis. Researchers link heavy editing and platform use to body preoccupation and surgery consideration, though causation is unproven. Surgeons are urged to screen for BDD, and cosmetic surgery is not considered a treatment for it.

angle.text: The term describes people who want to look like their filtered selfies, which drives interest in cosmetic procedures and in how photos are framed. Studies link filter use to body dissatisfaction and surgery interest, though it is an informal term and not a formal diagnosis.

lead: Social media dysmorphia, also called Snapchat dysmorphia, filter dysmorphia or selfie dysmorphia, is an informal term for the phenomenon of people seeking cosmetic procedures to resemble their filtered or edited selfies, or feeling distress at the gap between their real appearance and edited images of themselves.[1] It is not a formal diagnosis. Clinicians discuss it in relation to body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), an obsessive preoccupation with perceived flaws in appearance.[1]

The term was coined by British cosmetic surgeon Tijion Esho, who observed that patients had shifted from bringing photos of celebrities to bringing edited images of themselves.[1] Research links heavy use of image-based platforms and photo-editing to body dissatisfaction and greater willingness to consider cosmetic surgery, though much of the evidence is correlational.[1]
infobox: Informal term, not a formal diagnosis

paras: Filters on apps such as Snapchat and Instagram can smooth skin, narrow noses and enlarge eyes in real time, producing an idealised version of the user's face.[1] Commentators say this can set unrealistic standards and widen the perceived gap between a person's actual and filtered appearance.[1] A related aesthetic, sometimes called 'Instagram Face', is described as combining features such as high cheekbones, poreless skin and a small nose.[1]

Esho has said that patients previously presented photos of celebrities or models as reference images, but by the late 2010s many brought heavily edited selfies.[1] Researchers at Boston Medical Center also linked the rise of Snapchat, launched in 2011, to patients requesting surgery to look like filtered images.[1]

A 2019 study in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery (Chen and colleagues) reported that people who used image-focused platforms and photo-editing apps were more likely to consider cosmetic surgery.[1] A 2015 study by McLean and colleagues found adolescent girls who edited photos of themselves and invested heavily in their images reported more body preoccupation and eating concerns.[1] A systematic review by Ryding and Kuss (2019) examined links between social networking use, body dissatisfaction and BDD.[1] Most of these studies are observational, so they do not establish causation. A 2022 survey by the American Academy of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery reported that most surveyed surgeons had patients seeking improvement for selfie appearance.[1]

Body image researcher Jasmine Fardouly has argued that negative body image is strongly tied to photo editing.[1] The authors of the JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery paper urged surgeons to screen patients for BDD before operating, and clinical commentary cited on Wikipedia states that cosmetic surgery is not a treatment for BDD.[1] Some of the statistics widely quoted in coverage originate from advocacy campaigns rather than peer-reviewed studies.[1]

In August 2020 Instagram banned filters that directly promote cosmetic surgery, after criticism of a filter that let users mark up their faces as a surgeon would.[1] Dove's #NoDigitalDistortion campaign aims to build self-esteem among young people.[1] Critics have said platform owners have done little more to limit distortion filters.[1]

Filtered and edited faces are part of the background against which online appearance communities discuss looks, ratings and procedures. Community-specific claims about filters are not covered by the sources reviewed here.
